note: Bet B6, 'The other shore' (docs/council/2026-11-23-two-day-plan.md): the decade told from Carthage's side, as a second chronicle. It reads only the game's log: each rule below turns one kind of log line into a sentence in Carthage's voice, and every sentence keeps the numbers of the log lines it came from. The voice, the wording and the choice of what Carthage would record are invention. Lines tagged history follow a passage in Diodorus or Aristotle, quoted in docs/research/carthage-chronicle.md. Nothing here changes the game.
opening: Here is set down what befell Carthage in the ten years after the peace with the tyrant of Syracuse, as the city's own record might have kept it: the council's votes, the generals it chose, the gods' favour and their anger. The Greeks wrote their histories of these years. Carthage's are lost, so this one is made from what happened in your game, and nothing else.

yearHead.source: The Marseille Tariff (a Carthaginian temple inscription of the third century BC, found at Marseille), lines 1 to 2
yearHead.two: In the time of the suffetes {a} and {b}
yearHead.one: In the time of the suffetes {a} and his colleague, whose name is not recorded
yearHead.none: In a year whose suffetes are not recorded

stillWriting: The record is still being written.

rules.match: ^Carthage's council turns to a new goal: War on the tyrant
say: The kings and the Elders could not agree, so the question of war went before the people, as the law allows. The people voted for war on the tyrant.
The Elders spoke against war, but they could not carry the kings with them, and the matter went to the people. The people chose war on the tyrant.

rules.match: ^Carthage's council turns to a new goal: War on the tyrant
say: The council and the Elders agreed: Carthage would make war on the tyrant of Syracuse.
The council resolved on war with the tyrant, and the Elders were of one mind with it.

rules.match: ^Carthage's council turns to a new goal: Guard the tribute
say: The council resolved to hold what the peace had given: the tribute of the Greek towns and the strongholds of the west.
The Hundred urged the council to keep a firm hand on Sicily, and the council resolved to guard the tribute.

rules.match: ^Carthage's council turns to a new goal: Rebuild
say: The council turned to mending what plague and war had broken, and to trade.
The Elders had their way: no new war, but ships, silver and the harbour first.

rules.match: ^Carthage's council turns to a new goal: Peace at a price
say: In the council the Elders said aloud what many thought: Sicily was costing more than it was worth. The council sought peace.
The council voted to seek peace with the tyrant, at a price if it must.

rules.match: ^Carthage's council turns to a new goal: Quiet Libya
say: The council turned from Sicily to Libya, where Carthage's own fields were in revolt.
Sicily could wait. The council's whole care was now for Libya, which had risen.
Heralds went out: Carthage was at war with Syracuse.
War was proclaimed against the tyrant of Syracuse.

rules.quote: When it had been read in the council and subsequently before the people, it came about that the Carthaginians were not a little distressed at the thought of war
rules.match: ^(You declare war on Carthage|Syracuse is at war with Carthage)[.]
say: A herald came from the tyrant with a letter for the council: Syracuse would make war on Carthage unless Carthage let the Greek cities go. It was read in the council and then before the people, and the city was afraid.
The tyrant's herald stood before the council and read his master's letter: war, unless Carthage gave up the Greek cities. When it was read before the people, there was fear in the streets.

rules.match: ^The council gives ([A-Z][a-z]+) sole command of the war[.]
say: The council made {1} king by law, and gave the whole war into his hands.
By the law of the city {1} was made king for the war, with sole command over it.
{1} crossed to Sicily and landed at {2} with about {3|k} men.
The fleet carried {1} over the sea to {2}, and about {3|k} men with him.
The tyrant's ships fell on the transports in the crossing, and about {2|k} men went down with them.
On the crossing the Greek warships caught the transports. About {2|k} men were drowned.
There was no silver for the hired men, and about {2|k} of them left {1}'s camp.
{1}'s mercenaries were not paid, and about {2|k} went home.
Plague in the camp took about {2|k} of {1}'s men.
Hunger thinned {1}'s army by about {2|k} men.

rules.quote: The Siceli, who had hated Dionysius from of old and now had an opportunity to revolt, went over in a body
say: The Sicels of the hills, who had always hated the tyrant, came over to {1}, about {2|k} of them.
{1}'s army grew by about {2|k} men.

rules.quote: they gathered armaments from all Libya as well as from Iberia
rules.match: ^Carthage calls up its Libyan subjects[.] [(]about ([0-9,]+) men[.][)]
say: The villages of Libya gave up their sons to the levy, about {1|k} men. They did not give them gladly.
About {1|k} Libyans were called to the levy, and their fathers cursed the dues and the call alike.

rules.quote: dispatched members of the senate with large sums of money to recruit mercenaries in Europe
rules.match: ^Carthage sends men with silver to hire soldiers abroad[.] [(]about ([0-9,]+) men hired[.][)]
say: Members of the council sailed with silver to hire soldiers overseas, and came back with about {1|k} men.
Silver went out with men of the council to the hiring grounds over the sea; about {1|k} soldiers came back for it.
Men were sent to strengthen {list}.
The garrisons of {list} were made stronger.
The merchant ships went out along the coasts and came home again, and silver came in with them.
Trade went on: the ships sailed, the harbour was full, and the treasury filled.
The merchant houses sent their ships out, and the city lived by the sea as it always had.
In the harbour the yards built warships and transports.
New hulls went down the slips in the war harbour, warships and transports.

rules.quote: may dwell in their cities, which shall be unfortified, but shall pay tribute to the Carthaginians
rules.match: ^The tribute of ([0-9]+) Sicilian towns? reaches Carthage[.]
say: The tribute of {1|n} Sicilian {1|towns} came in, as the peace laid down.
From Sicily came the tribute of {1|n} Greek {1|towns}, by the terms of the peace.
The treasury was empty, and hired men who were not paid went home.
There was no silver to pay the mercenaries, and some of them left.

rules.match: ^Carthage makes offerings to win back the gods[.]
say: Offerings were made in every temple of the city, to win back the gods.
The council ordered offerings at the great sanctuaries, to Baal Hammon and to Tanit, Face of Baal, so that the gods would turn back to the city.
To quiet the Libyans, the council let a year's dues go unpaid.
The council forgave Libya a year's dues, to buy back its quiet.

rules.quote: the pestilence continued to rage no less in Libya also and great numbers both of the Carthaginians themselves and of their allies were struck down
rules.match: ^Plague breaks out in Carthage and in Libya[.]
say: Plague came into the city and spread through Libya, and great numbers died, citizens and allies alike. Men said the gods were angry.
The plague came back, in the city and in the Libyan villages. The dead were many, and the priests said the gods were not yet satisfied.
The plague left the city at last.
The sickness burned itself out, and the city counted its dead.

rules.source: Diodorus 14.77.1 (the game's own rendering of the Greek)
rules.quote: οἱ σύμμαχοι καὶ πάλαι μὲν μισοῦντες τὸ βάρος τῆς τῶν Καρχηδονίων ἡγεμονίας
say: The Libyans rose. They had long hated the weight of Carthage's rule, and now they took up arms against it.
Libya revolted. The subjects had hated the burden of Carthage's rule for many years, and the levies were the last of it.
Libya was quiet again.
The Libyan villages laid down their arms.

rules.match: ^In Carthage, the Libyan subjects sour to (Angry|Rebellious)[.]
say: The Libyans grew angry: their sons had been taken for the levy.
In Libya the villages muttered against the levy that had taken their sons.

rules.match: ^In Carthage, the (Elders|Hundred|people of Carthage) sour to (Angry|Rebellious)[.]
say: When word of the sacrilege reached the city, the {1} were angry.

say: The siege of {2} went on.
{1} kept {2} shut in, and waited for hunger to do the work.
{1} lifted the siege of {2}.

say: The siege lines before {1} were pushed closer to the walls.
{1}'s men went up against the walls of {2}.
{1} sent the army against the walls of {2}.

say: The assault on {1} was thrown back.
The walls of {1} held, and the men came back down the ladders.

rules.match: ^([A-Z][a-z]+) submits to Carthage and is spared[.]
say: {1} opened its gates and was spared.
{1} gave itself up, and Carthage spared it.

rules.match: ^([A-Z][a-z]+) sacks ([A-Z][a-z]+)[.] Its people flee to the hills[.]
say: {1} took {2} by storm and gave it to the soldiers. Its people fled to the hills.
{2} was stormed and sacked by {1}'s army, and its people scattered into the mountains.
{1} came over to Carthage of its own will.
{1} left the tyrant and joined Carthage.
{w1} stopped paying its tribute and went over to the tyrant. In the council, men called it theft.
{w1} was lost to the tyrant, and its tribute with it.
Word came that the tyrant had put his own soldiers into {w1}.
At {2} the gods gave {1} the victory over the tyrant.
{1} met the tyrant's army at {2} and beat it.
At {1} the tyrant's army had the better of ours.
The army was beaten by the tyrant at {1}.
A battle was fought, and neither side gave way.
{1}'s army was lost in Sicily.
Of {1}'s army, nothing came home.
The tyrant's army was destroyed.
The tyrant lost his whole army in the field.

rules.match: ^([A-Z][a-z]+) comes home to Carthage in disgrace[.]
say: {1} came home in disgrace.
{1} came back to the city, and no one met him at the harbour.

rules.quote: he went about the temples of the city in the cheapest clothing, charging himself with impiety
rules.match: ^Himilcon goes about the temples of Carthage in rags
say: Himilcon went about the temples of the city in the poorest clothes, charging himself with impiety before the gods. Then he passed sentence on himself, and starved himself to death.
Himilcon walked from temple to temple in rags and named himself guilty before the gods. In the end he refused food until he died.
The council stripped {1} of his command.
{1}'s command was taken from him by the council.

rules.match: ^The story takes[.] ([A-Z][a-z]+) is recalled to answer for it[.]
say: It was said in the city that {1} was in the tyrant's pay. He was called home to answer for it.
The council called {1}'s army home from {2}.
The council sent ships to bring {1}'s army back from {2}.
{1}'s army sailed home.
{1} fell back from {2} to {3}.

rules.match: ^([A-Z][a-z]+) takes command of the army in ([A-Z][a-z]+)[.]
say: {1} took command of the army in {2}.
Another {1|k} men were shipped across to {2}.
The council sent {2} about {1|k} more men.
The fleet carried grain to the army in Sicily.
Ships kept the army in Sicily fed from Libya.

rules.match: ^([A-Z][a-z]+)'s army eats the last of its food[.]
say: {1}'s army ate the last of its grain.

rules.match: ^Carthage's envoys come to Syracuse with terms
say: Envoys sailed to the tyrant with terms: peace, and each side to keep what it held.
The council sent envoys to Syracuse to offer peace on the terms of things as they stood.

rules.match: ^Peace is made between Syracuse and Carthage[.]
say: Peace was made with the tyrant. Each side kept what it held.
The war ended in a peace: each side kept what it had.
Syracuse fell. The tyrant fled over the sea with what he could carry.
The city of the tyrant was taken, and the tyrant ran to his ships.
The tyrant threw his army against the walls of {1}.
The tyrant laid siege to {1}.

rules.quote: he also sold as booty the Motyans who survived
rules.match: ^Your soldiers sack (Motya|Panormus) and sell its people[.]
say: {1} was taken and sacked. The Greeks killed whoever they met, and those who lived were sold. In Carthage the families of {1} put on mourning.

rules.match: ^Your soldiers sack ([A-Z][a-z]+) and sell its people[.]
say: The tyrant sacked {1} and sold its people.
{1} was sacked by the tyrant, and its people sold as slaves.
{1} was lost to the tyrant.
An envoy of the tyrant came with gifts and was heard in the council.
A Greek envoy spoke before the council, and his gifts were accepted.
An envoy of the tyrant was sent away with nothing.
A friend in Syracuse sent news, and the council acted on it.
Word came from Carthage's paid man in the tyrant's city, and the council believed it.

rules.match: ^Carthage's general believes ([A-Z][a-z]+)'s report and marches on a lie[.]
say: {1}, a captain who had taken Carthage's silver, sent word to the general, and the army marched on it.

rules.quote: manned forty triremes during the night with the citizens of Carthage and began his flight, abandoning all the rest of his army
rules.match: ^On the fourth night the Carthaginians slip away
say: On the fourth night the citizens of Carthage were taken off by ship in the dark. The hired men and the allies were left behind.

rules.match: ^Beaten and sick, ([A-Z][a-z]+) sends to you in secret
say: {1}, beaten and sick, sent in secret to the tyrant: let the Carthaginians go home by night, and the silver in the camp would be his.

rules.quote: the plague first attacked the Libyans
say: Plague came into the camp before {1}. It took the Libyans first, and soon no one would go near the sick.

rules.match: ^Plague breaks out in the camp before ([A-Z][a-z]+)[.]
say: Plague broke out in the camp before {1}.

rules.match: ^Plague breaks out in the camp before ([A-Z][a-z]+)[.]
say: Plague broke out in the tyrant's camp before {1}. In Carthage they said the gods remembered the temples he had robbed.

rules.quote: Himilcon seized the suburb of Achradinê; and he also plundered the temples of both Demeter and Corê
rules.match: ^Carthage's soldiers have taken the suburb of Achradina
say: The army took the suburb of Achradina, and the soldiers stripped the temple of the Greeks' goddesses, Demeter and Kore.

rules.quote: Himilcon decked his ships with the spoils taken from the enemy and put in at the great harbour of the Syracusans
rules.match: ^Carthage's fleet rows into the Great Harbour
say: The fleet rowed into the Great Harbour of Syracuse in order, decked with the spoils of the tyrant's ships, and the merchantmen came in behind it in their hundreds.

rules.quote: The Carthaginians, against whom the gods were clearly fighting
rules.match: ^Ships from Africa bring word that Carthage is in mourning
say: The city was in mourning, and believed the gods were fighting against it. Men gathered in little groups and begged the god to end his anger. The council voted to make peace with every god who had been wronged: Demeter and Kore were given priests from the first families, and rites in the Greek manner.

rules.match: ^Merchants from Carthage say that (.+?), a man of the Hundred, has risen in the council to demand that ([A-Z][a-z]+) answer for the war
say: {1}, a man of the Hundred, rose in the council and demanded that {2} answer for the war.

rules.match: ^A trader brings a quiet word from (.+?), head of one of Carthage's great merchant houses
say: {1}, head of a great merchant house, sent quiet word to the tyrant by a trader: spare Carthage's merchant ships, and he would speak for peace among the Elders.

rules.match: ^Word comes that (.+?), who speaks for the dockyards in Carthage's assembly
say: {1}, who speaks for the dockyards, had the assembly shouting for vengeance.

rules.match: ^Your watchers report that a Carthaginian merchant has been carrying silver to (.+?)'s house by night[.]
say: A Carthaginian merchant carried silver by night to the house of {list} in Syracuse.

rules.match: ^Envoys from Carthage have been seen at the house of ([A-Z][a-z]+), the first man of ([A-Z][a-z]+)[.]
say: Envoys went to {1}, the first man of {2}, with gifts, and reminded him what happened to towns that trusted Syracuse.
{1} sent Carthage's envoys home.
In the city, death came to the great houses: {list}.
The houses of Carthage mourned {list}.

rules.match: ^(.+?), of Carthage now heads the house and is (.+)[.]$
say: {1} took up the headship of the house: {2}.
In the Sicilian towns, {list} died.
Some seasons the council did nothing, and counted its silver.

rules.match: ^The sword falls[.] You are killed by men you trusted[.] (.+?) led them[.]
say: Word came over the sea: the tyrant of Syracuse was dead, cut down by men he trusted. {1|cap} led them.

rules.match: ^The plotters seize the Island[.] You escape with your life and go into exile[.] (.+?) led them[.]
say: Word came that the tyrant had been driven out of his fortress by his own people, and had fled. {1|cap} led them.
Word came that the tyrant no longer ruled Syracuse: {1} had taken his place.

rules.match: ^You ride out of Syracuse on your swiftest horse
say: Word came that the tyrant had ridden out of Syracuse on his fastest horse, and his rule was over.
Word came that the tyrant had laid down his power and lived on in Syracuse as a private man. Few in Carthage believed it.

closings.say: So the tyrant's city fell, and the temples Carthage had lost were repaid. Let it be written that Carthage waited, and did not forget.

closings.needs: ^(The sword falls|The plotters seize the Island|.+ takes your place: |You ride out of Syracuse|You lay down your power)
closings.say: So the tyrant was gone, not by Carthage's hand but by his own city's. In the council the Elders said that the gods are patient.

closings.needs: ^Himilcon goes about the temples of Carthage in rags
closings.say: The record of these years closes in mourning. The tyrant still held Syracuse, and Carthage had learned to fear the gods it had wronged.

closings.needs: ^(Carthage declares war on Syracuse|You declare war on Carthage|Syracuse is at war with Carthage)[.]
closings.unlessLater: ^Peace is made between Syracuse and Carthage[.]
closings.say: The ten years ended, and the war with the tyrant was not finished. The yards were busy, and the council was still at war.

closings.needs: ^Peace is made between Syracuse and Carthage[.]
closings.say: The ten years ended in a peace. The tyrant still held Syracuse; Carthage still held the west. Each side counted its losses and built ships.
Ten years passed, and Carthage never went to war with the tyrant. It traded, took its tribute, and waited.

greekYears.text: The Greek histories say that after the peace the Carthaginians sailed home, having lost more than half their soldiers to plague, and that the plague went on in Libya.
greekYears.quote: the Carthaginians sailed off to Libya, having lost more than half their soldiers from the plague

greekYears.text: The Greek histories say that the plague had destroyed the larger part of Libya's people, and that when Syracuse voted for war its people plundered the property of the Carthaginians who lived among them.
greekYears.quote: the Syracusans, with the permission of Dionysius, seized as plunder the property of the Phoenicians

greekYears.text: The Greek histories say that the tyrant's letter was read in the council and then before the people, and that Carthage, unprepared, made Himilcon king by law and gathered armies from all Libya and Iberia.
The Greek histories say that plague destroyed Himilcon's army before Syracuse, that he starved himself to death in Carthage, and that the city believed the gods were fighting against it.
greekYears.quote: The Carthaginians, against whom the gods were clearly fighting

greekSilent: The Greek histories say nothing of Carthage in this year.
